newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian labour challenges pro-investment policy.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian labour challenges pro-investment policy.

text.p: Cambodia's flourishing garment sector, which turns out everything from overalls to denim hot pants, was until one month ago heralded as an economic success story for this war-scarred nation.

But after nearly a dozen worker protests that have brought repeated work stoppages and clashes with police, the fortunes of those in the fashion business may prove as fleeting as the latest styles, industry observers said.
"This is causing big damage to the Cambodian economy," said Van Sou Ieng, chairman of the Cambodian Garment Manufacturers' Association.

He warned that the growing momentum of the workers' movement was creating havoc for manufacturers and jeopardising Cambodia's fastest-growing industrial sector -- with 38 factories and more than 16,000 workers.
The industry's troubles in recent weeks have been dramatic, analysts agreed, but not surprising.

After several years of tuning out mounting complaints from workers over poor working conditions, Cambodia has found its policy of investors first, labour second, has given birth to a modern labour movement -- with the garment sector as just its first target, they said.
"Cambodian labour is going through terrible growing pains right now," said one international labour analyst.
"There has been so much focus here on economic issues and not on social issues. If you do that, the social issues are going to bite you in the back," the analyst said.
The bite for the garment industry has come from opposition leader Sam Rainsy, who founded a garment workers union last month.

"Cambodia was a paradise for garment manufacturers -- until last month," Sam Rainsy said, citing the country's cheap labour, attractive investment incentives and minimal regulations. "They are not prepared to respect the process of democratisation at the grass-roots level."
But because he has led nearly all of the recent protests, some have suggested the movement is not a grass-roots effort but rather is politically motivated.

A former finance minister, Sam Rainsy was expelled from the royalist FUNCINPEC party and the National Assembly in 1995 for alleging widespread corruption and human rights abuses in the government. He has since been an outspoken critic of the ruling coalition, which has refused to recognise the Khmer Nation Party he formed after his expulsion.

"It's not in the nature of Cambodia to have this kind of labour unrest. Normally, Cambodians do not have demonstrations. I hope it's not someone doing this for their political gain," said Sun Chanthol, secretary-general of the Council for the Development of Cambodia, the government's centre for private investment.

Yet regardless of Sam Rainsy's motives, analysts said his work has forced the government to consider labour issues such as child labour and sexism in the workplace and reports by human rights groups of appalling conditions in garment factories.
